source: Hellas et al. (2023) Exploring the Responses of LLMs to Beginner Programmers' Help Requests (ICER)
finding: Models were given real novice help requests with buggy code and asked to find the issues. They usually found something real, rarely everything, and often invented problems.
numbers: GPT-3.5, English prompts, 30 responses: at least one real issue 90%; all real issues 57%; non-existent issue 40%. Codex: 70%, 13%, 40%.
limits: Small comparison sample (30 responses per model-language pair); one Finnish programming course; 2022-23 models.
agent_relevance: A debugging agent must expect that a confident diagnosis of novice-style buggy code is wrong or padded with false issues about 4 times in 10. Add a verify step before acting on any diagnosis.

source: Hellas et al. (2023) Help Requests: extended GPT-3.5 analysis
finding: Across 150 help requests (275 issues, 1.9 per request) GPT-3.5 found a real issue in most, all issues in about half, and false issues in nearly half. It nearly always wrote code.
numbers: 150 requests, 15 exercises: at least one real issue 123/150; all issues named in 82 of those; false issue in 72 requests (48%); code included 99%; model-solution quality code 65%. Themes: logic 72%, I/O 34%, syntax 8%.
limits: Single course (Dart), single model; manual labelling by the authors.
agent_relevance: The model solves instead of hinting. A fluent fix is not evidence that the fault was found.

source: Hellas et al. (2023) Help Requests: accuracy by novice error type
finding: Model accuracy depended on the kind of novice error. Conditionals were worst, loops best.
numbers: Share of requests where GPT-3.5 addressed ALL issues: conditionals 35%, iteration 73%, arithmetic 57%, output formatting 44%, unwanted output 54%, missing output 50%. Across exercises, all issues addressed in 1/10 responses at worst and 10/10 at best (with 4/10 false positives even then).
limits: Many requests have more than one issue and the table does not match each response to a specific issue; exercise effects have no clear pattern.
agent_relevance: Faults in branching logic are where reading code is weakest. Route such faults to execution and tests.

source: Hellas et al. (2023) Help Requests: instruction following and pedagogy
finding: Told not to give code, GPT-3.5 gave code anyway. Some advice was off-course or unsuitable for very incomplete code.
numbers: Code in 99-100% of GPT-3.5 responses despite the instruction; Codex included code 33% (English). 17 of 150 responses (over 10%) suggested features outside the course. All 6 'very incomplete' programs got pedagogically unsuitable replies.
limits: The prompt asked for no code; other prompt wordings might do better (authors tuned the prompt first).
agent_relevance: Constraints written in a prompt are not guardrails. Enforce 'no solution' with a separate check or pipeline stage (see CodeHelp, TreeInstruct).

source: Leinonen et al. (2022) Using Large Language Models to Enhance Programming Error Messages
finding: Codex rewrote Python error messages for novices. The text was readable but the explanation and fix were often wrong.
numbers: 162 outputs (9 error messages x 3 program types x 2 temperatures x 3 samples). Averages: comprehensible 88%, has explanation 84%, explanation correct 48%, has fix 70%, fix correct 33%, improvement over original 54%, unnecessary content 32%. Correct explanation ranged from 11% (unexpected EOF) to 83% (can't assign to function call).
limits: Codex, Python only, two raters, short programs. Temperature 0 gave better improvement (over 70%) than 0.7 (up to 50%).
agent_relevance: Reading a failure message correctly is a core debugging step and the model got it right under half the time. Use low temperature on diagnostic steps.

source: Phung et al. (2023) Generative AI for Programming Education: Benchmarking ChatGPT, GPT-4, and Human Tutors
finding: GPT-4 repaired buggy novice programs and gave hints much better than ChatGPT but stayed below human tutors on harder tasks.
numbers: 5 Python problems, 25 instances per scenario. Program repair Correct: ChatGPT 68%, GPT-4 88%, tutor 100%; GPT-4 made more edits (36.6 tokens vs 19.0). Hint generation Overall quality: ChatGPT 18%, GPT-4 66%.
limits: Only 25 instances per scenario, five easy problems, expert annotation; Fibonacci hardest.
agent_relevance: Repair is easier than minimal repair: models over-edit. A debugging loop should prefer the smallest change that makes the failing test pass.

source: Phung et al. (2023) Benchmark: grading feedback and task synthesis
finding: Tasks needing a deep model of the novice's bug were far worse: matching a tutor's grade and building a simpler problem that shows the same bug.
numbers: Grading feedback Match: ChatGPT 10%, GPT-4 16%, tutor 52%. Task synthesis Overall: ChatGPT 10%, GPT-4 22%, tutor 74%; weakest on 'SimilarBugs'.
limits: Same 25-instance setup.
agent_relevance: Abstracting a bug to its underlying misconception is a skill the models lack. Do not rely on them to state the transferable lesson.

source: Phung et al. (2023) Benchmark: pair programming and contextualised explanation
finding: Explaining correct code was easy. Completing partial novice code while keeping the student's context was medium.
numbers: Pair programming Overall: ChatGPT 38%, GPT-4 64%, tutor 82% (GPT-4 rewrote the student's context). Contextualised explanation Overall: ChatGPT 72%, GPT-4 84%, tutor 92%.
limits: Explanation inputs were short bug-free programs for popular problems, which the authors say makes it easy.
agent_relevance: Models are strong when code is correct and weak when it is wrong. Fault finding should not be framed as explanation.

source: Phung et al. (2023) Automating Human Tutor-Style Programming Feedback: GPT4Hints-GPT3.5Val
finding: A two-model pipeline raised hint quality to tutor level. GPT-4 writes a hint using failing tests and the fix. A weaker GPT-3.5 'student' tries to use the hint. The hint is kept only if the student succeeds.
numbers: Plain GPT-4 hint quality about 60% vs human tutors over 90%. Pipeline precision about 95% (94.7, 97.6, 95.5 on three datasets) with coverage over 70% (76.0, 87.5, 73.3).
limits: Needs failing test cases and a reference fix as input; hints are withheld for some programs (coverage below 100%).
agent_relevance: A template for an agent loop: a simulated novice tests whether an explanation transfers before it is shown. It costs coverage and buys precision.

source: Phung et al. (2023) GPT4Hints-GPT3.5Val ablations
finding: Repeated trials and a weaker student model mattered. One trial gave low coverage. A GPT-4 student validated worse.
numbers: First dataset: default precision 94.7 / coverage 76.0; single trial k=1: 91.7 / 48.0; GPT-4 as student: 89.3 / 56.0.
limits: Three datasets; effect sizes differ across them.
agent_relevance: Use several independent trials for any 'does this advice work' check and choose the checker model on purpose.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) Studying the Effect of AI Code Generators on Supporting Novice Learners (CHI)
finding: In a 10-session controlled experiment with 69 novices aged 10-17, access to Codex helped code authoring and did not hurt later manual code modification.
numbers: N=69, 45 tasks. Codex group: 1.15x progress, 1.8x correctness (d=1.67, p<.001), 0.57x time, fewer errors per task (1.28 vs 2.17, d=0.74), syntax errors 0.87 vs 1.67 (d=0.88). Documentation use 22.1% vs 54.3% (d=1.33). No decrease on modification tasks.
limits: Short training, Codex 2022 model, children, small tasks; immediate post-test showed no difference.
agent_relevance: Tool help removes syntax friction but can hide the thinking. Debugging scaffolds for an agent should keep the hypothesis step explicit.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) Codex study: retention and prior skill
finding: One week later the Codex group did slightly better but not significantly. Low-skill learners seemed to gain more.
numbers: Retention authoring 59.1% vs 49.8% (d=0.28, p=.262); modifying 47.5% vs 34.8% (d=0.41, p=.092). Codex group made more errors on retention authoring (1.58 vs 0.99, d=0.51, p=.042).
limits: Sub-groups about 17-18 learners; main retention effects not significant.
agent_relevance: No clear evidence of harm or benefit to retention. Do not claim a learning benefit from this study alone.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) How Novices Use LLM-Based Code Generators to Solve CS1 Coding Tasks
finding: Log analysis of 33 learners shows novices mostly ask the model to write the whole solution, often with no attempt first. Using it to fix code was rare but often well localised.
numbers: 33 learners, 45 tasks. Prompts at task start 46% (n=760), of which 92% (n=703) with no own attempt. Full task description pasted 66% (n=503). Uses: entire solution 43%, new subgoals 37%, fix code 7% (n=110); when fixing, 61% (n=73) localised the issue correctly.
limits: Qualitative coding, one self-paced platform, ages 10-17.
agent_relevance: Novices skip hypothesis and localisation and go straight to repair. An agent that copies this would repair without a diagnosis.

source: Prather et al. (2023) 'It's Weird That it Knows What I Want': Copilot for Novice Programmers
finding: First observation study of CS1 students using Copilot. Students got lost between suggestions and tasks, struggled with metacognition, and some accepted code unchanged.
numbers: 19 students (C++), observation plus interviews; 13 participants accepted just-generated code without changes at least once.
limits: Small n, one university, qualitative.
agent_relevance: Accepting output without verification is the failure; make verification a mandatory state in an agent loop.

source: Prather et al. (2024) The Widening Gap: Benefits and Harms of Generative AI for Novice Programmers
finding: Replicates an earlier lab study of novice metacognitive difficulties, adding GenAI. Strong students accelerated. Struggling students kept the old difficulties, got new ones, and felt falsely competent.
numbers: 21 lab sessions (observation, interview, eye tracking); 20 of 21 completed the task; ten participants struggled. Struggling students thought they performed better than they did.
limits: Small lab sample, one problem, qualitative.
agent_relevance: Misplaced confidence after a plausible answer is the central harm. Calibration checks matter for the agent too.

source: Liffiton et al. (2023) CodeHelp: Using LLMs with Guardrails for Scalable Support in Programming Classes
finding: A deployed help tool that tells students what is wrong without writing solution code, using structured prompts and instructor-set topic limits.
numbers: 52 students, 12 weeks, 45 survey responses (87%). About 80% of the class sent 10 or more queries, about 50% sent 30 or more; 70% used it in four or more weeks.
limits: One first-year course, no learning-outcome measure, self-selected survey.
agent_relevance: A working agent-loop pattern: stage prompts, forbid code blocks, refuse off-topic or solution-seeking input.

source: Liffiton et al. (2023) CodeHelp design: one-shot requests
finding: Each query is a one-shot request independent of others, because the chance of an off-the-rails answer grows with more rounds.
numbers: Design choice; no effect size reported in the text read.
quote: likelihood ... increases with additional rounds of user input and model response
limits: Contrasts with multi-turn Socratic tutors.
agent_relevance: A trade-off to record: long-dialogue drift versus guided discovery.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2024) CodeAid: Evaluating a Classroom Deployment of an LLM-based Programming Assistant
finding: CodeAid gives conceptual answers, pseudo-code and annotated fixes without full code. Deployed to a 700-student class; 8,132 usages logged.
numbers: 700 students, 12 weeks, 563 consented; 1,750 usages coded. Coding-scheme agreement 82-94% (kappa .61-.92). Query types include buggy code resolution and error message interpretation.
limits: Survey and interview study; no test-score effect measured in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Buggy-code resolution and error-message interpretation are common novice requests. Test the agent on these.

source: Lyu et al. (2024) Evaluating the Effectiveness of LLMs in Introductory CS Education: A Semester-Long Field Study
finding: A semester-long between-subjects study found score gains with an LLM tutor, mainly for students new to LLM tools.
numbers: 50 students. Score change pre-test to final: experimental +12.50, control -3.17. Paired pre vs final for experimental p=.026. Students new to LLM tools: g=0.69, p=0.03 (n=42 in that comparison).
limits: Small n, final exam taken without the tool, authors note gap between expected and actual student ability.
agent_relevance: One of few outcome studies; effect is modest and uneven.

source: Al-Hossami et al. (2024) Instruct, Not Assist: TreeInstruct, Socratic code debugging with state-space planning
finding: An instructor agent keeps a tree of student misunderstandings (conceptual and syntactic) and asks probing questions instead of giving the fix.
numbers: Preferred by experts about 78% of the time (79.43% vs BRIDGE, 77.43% vs Vanilla). Student fixes code 24.55% more. In multi-bug settings success up 16.6% (syntactic) and 11.59% (conceptual). New benchmark of 150 expert-annotated bugs.
limits: Mostly simulated students plus a small human test; Socratic questions alone reach at most 77.27% success.
agent_relevance: A direct use of a novice-misconception model in an LLM loop: keep explicit state of what is known and wrong, and plan the next question from it.

source: Al-Hossami et al. (2024) TreeInstruct ablations and multi-bug scaling
finding: Removing the explicit state representation hurt most. The baseline fell as bugs multiplied while TreeInstruct held.
numbers: Vanilla drops 14.55% from 1-bug to 3-bug; TreeInstruct drops 2.44% (Socratic Debugging Benchmark to 1-bug) and 1.53% (1-bug to 3-bug). One ablation without state grounding: success -18.25%, relevance -46.63%, logic -51.39%. Vanilla gives the most direct hints.
limits: Percentages as reported; LLM-based judges used.
agent_relevance: Interdependent faults need an explicit fault ledger. Supports tracking several suspected faults at once.

source: Zhang et al. (2022) Repairing Bugs in Python Assignments Using Large Language Models (MMAPR)
finding: A Codex system combining multi-modal prompts, iterative querying, few-shot examples from peers' programs and chunking repaired most real student programs.
numbers: 286 real student programs. Baseline (BIFI + Refactory) 67.13%; MMAPR without few-shot 86.71%; with few-shot 96.50%. Iterative querying raised 82.87% to 86.71%. Temperature 0.8.
limits: Codex-era model, introductory assignments with tests, small patches required.
agent_relevance: Iteration plus retrieval of similar earlier fixes is a recipe an agent loop can copy.

source: Savelka et al. (2023) LLMs (GPT) Struggle to Answer Multiple-Choice Questions about Code
finding: Models write programs from text but fail more at questions that need tracing or output prediction.
numbers: 530 MCQs, 3 Python courses. text-davinci-003 65.5% overall; with code 59.5% vs 77.9% without (p<0.0001). Fill-in and completion items did best; analysis and 'what is the output' items worst.
limits: GPT-3 era models; MCQ format.
agent_relevance: Code tracing, the skill behind mental execution, is a weak point. Hand tracing to a real interpreter.

source: Babe et al. (2023) StudentEval: A Benchmark of Student-Written Prompts for LLMs of Code
finding: 1,749 prompts by 80 novices for 48 problems show models are sensitive to beginner phrasing. Sampling noise can mislead students about their prompts.
numbers: Mean pass@1 for signatures without docstring 0.0519. Larger Code LLMs scored 2x or more of smaller ones on StudentEval. StarChat-Alpha about 10 points absolute above competitors on first/last success prompts.
limits: About prompting, not debugging; students had one semester of Python.
agent_relevance: Rerun a prompt several times before trusting a verdict, because one lucky sample misleads.

source: Leinonen et al. (2023) Comparing Code Explanations Created by Students and Large Language Models
finding: GPT-3 explanations were judged easier to understand and more accurate than student-written ones.
numbers: Probability that the LLM explanation was easier about 60% and more accurate about 56% in paired comparisons; some perception differences not significant after Bonferroni correction.
limits: Short mostly-correct functions; authors say bug detection is untested.
agent_relevance: Explaining correct code is a strength; do not generalise to faulty code.

source: Prather et al. (2022) Programming Is Hard - Or at Least It Used to Be
finding: Position paper that quotes how Codex performs on introductory problems and how wording changes results.
numbers: Quoted: Codex 29% of problems at first pass, 70% with repeated sampling; making a prompt more explicit raised correct samples from 12% to 55%; AlphaCode in top 54% of contestants.
limits: Position paper; numbers are quoted from other work.
agent_relevance: Background only: correctness depends on prompt wording.

source: Search gap: LLM misconception-aware tutors 2025-2026 (Crossref listing only)
finding: A 2026 ACM paper titled Misconception-Aware LLM Programming Tutor (lessons learned from student-tutor interactions) exists. So does Debugging with an AI Tutor (ICER 2024). Full text not accessible (HTTP 403), so no numbers.
limits: Only titles seen via Crossref; abstracts not retrieved; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate limited and WebSearch budget was used up. No study found that replays Murphy et al. (2008) categories on an LLM.
agent_relevance: Worth reading later. Relevant to a misconception ledger in a tutoring agent.
